For neither are things that will be continuous with one another; for what will be [will have come to be] in something atomic, just as what has come to be; for it has come to be in time, but it ceases coming to be and has come to be in something atomic. So between these too there <must> be time divisible to infinity. And in the case of things that will be, and of the deductions about them, one must take immediate premisses as the starting-point; for it does not follow that, if there is time between all things that will be, there is already something that will be between things that will be, just as neither [is there] something that has come to be between things that have come to be. Or he said 'immediate starting-point' instead of 'some last thing that bounds the things that will be, from which there is the ascent to the things that will be before it'. Or 'immediate starting-point' is to be taken instead of 'some premiss without a middle term, which is the starting-point of the deduction'. And he shows that the sequence described holds in this way also in the case of works and things, both those that have already come to be and those that will be.
p. 95b38 And since we see among things that come to be a certain coming to be in a circle.

Having said what position the cause has among causes in the strict sense, which he also called 'of the same kind', and what position among things that come to be successively, and having shown that what has been shown is borne out in the case of works too, since among works and among things that come to be there are also some <which> convert, so that not only does what came to be before it follow on the later, but also what comes after it follows on the first (for the coming to be of some things is in a circle), he speaks about these: which things can convert so as to become causes of one another, and in which cases coming to be in a circle occurs. And he shows that the cause of this is their being equal [in extension] and converting; for the words 'if the middle term and the extremes follow one another' indicate their being equal [in extension] and converting. For in the case of the house and the stones it does not convert; for it does not follow that, if the preparation of the stones follows on the coming to be of the house, the coming to be of the house also follows on the preparation of the stones. Nor does it in the case of causes of the same kind, as he said; for it does not follow that, if the screening by the earth is the cause of the eclipse, the eclipse is also the cause of the screening by the earth. And he says that circular proof and the conversion of causes occur in cases where the three terms of the deduction follow one another, being equal [in extension], and a different one is set down as middle term and cause at different times.
p. 96a8 Some things come to be universally; for it is always and in every case that something either is so or comes to be so.

Having shown, among things that come to be, in which cases the sequence is sound when it starts from the later things, and in which also from the first, as with things that come to be in a circle, he seems by these words to state the cause of the different sequences. For since some things that come to be come to be universally, which he explained by saying 'for it is always and in every case that something either is so or comes to be so' (for such is the universal), and others not always but for the most part (for most things that come to be by nature are of this sort), among things that come to be necessarily what comes after it follows also on the first, but no longer among contingent things; in their case the sound sequence is the one from the later things, as also in the case of all things that come to be by art. And for contingent conclusions in demonstrations the middle term too must be contingent; for if both premisses were universal, that is, necessary, the conclusion too would <necessarily> be necessary in any case; but it is supposed to be contingent. And just as in the other cases there are some immediate starting-points (deductive premisses) (for it is not possible for the middle terms of anything to be taken to infinity), so also in the case of contingent things and those that hold for the most part there will be some immediate premisses having as their starting-point that something is or comes to be for the most part.
p. 96a20 How, then, the 'what it is' is rendered into the terms.

That is, it is taken in the terms from which the deduction is made; for he has said that it is taken as the middle term in demonstrations. Or [it stands] instead of 'into the definitions'; for definitions that differ from demonstration in arrangement also take the 'what it is' of the thing, that is, the being of the thing, by taking the cause of its existence.
p. 96a21 And in what way there is or is not demonstration or definition of it, has been stated earlier.

Of the 'what it was to be', clearly, as he himself has said earlier. For it has been shown that there is no demonstration of the 'what it is' simply, but that it is taken in demonstration and made known through demonstration. Nor is there a definition of it of the sort that says 'an account which shows what the name signifies'. But of the other senses of definition, the most proper definition was 'an account differing from demonstration in arrangement'; for by taking the cause of the existence of the thing it also in a way showed the being of the thing. And so too [the definition] as starting-point of demonstration and [the definition] as conclusion; for these too are in a way definitions of the 'what it was to be'.
p. 96a22 How one must hunt for the things predicated in the 'what it is'.

He hands down to us a method by which we shall be able to hunt for and find the definition of each thing being investigated, since it is not possible to show it by demonstration. And since a definition is made from the things predicated in the 'what it is', that is, those in the substance, he says how we shall be able to take what is useful for the definitions of each thing. Of the things that belong to some things, some belong to certain things only, as being a starting-point to the unit and being without magnitude to the point, while others extend both to these and to other things, and more widely. And of those that extend more widely, some do not go beyond the genus of that of which we wish to take the things predicated in the 'what it is', while others extend also to things of a different genus; for animal and white do not belong in the same way to man. So of the things predicated universally, those which, though said more widely than the subject, do not extend more widely than its genus are taken as showing its substance and its 'what it was to be'. For of the things predicated more widely of something in this way, yet not going outside the genus in which that is of which the more widely predicated thing has been taken, if those are taken each of which is wider than the thing defined but all of which together belong to the thing defined alone and to all of it, these will show its substance. And the definition would be what produces something proper out of universal and common things.
p. 96a32 Such things, then, must be taken up to the point where so many are first taken.

First he shows that an account composed from the things predicated in the 'what it is' necessarily belongs to the subject, and second that it is also its definition. Instead of 'and the universals [are] necessary' one should read 'for the universals [are] necessary'; for he set down the universals' being necessary as the cause of the things predicated in the 'what it is' being necessary. For that the things predicated in the 'what it is' are predicated universally, being evident from its having been shown in the book before this (which he himself indicated by 'since it has been made clear to us in the earlier parts'), would be the [minor premiss], and the first premiss would be that universals are necessary. <This> too has been said in the first [book], and a little before he also said it thus: 'for this is the universal, what holds in every case and always'. And the conclusion that the things predicated in the 'what it is' are necessary would be drawn in the first figure through the universal as middle term.
p. 96b6 And that it is the substance is clear from the following.

Since it is not yet sufficient for being a definition that something be predicated in the 'what it is' and of necessity, and that this be those things, he shows that the account described is both substance and definition. For if it is not a definition but is predicated in the 'what it is', it would be a genus; for the proprium is not in the 'what it is', since it is an accident. If some name were assigned to this account, the genus would be named; but if it were not indicated by a name, it would be nameless. For some genera are nameless and are indicated by an account, such as 'land animal' or 'winged animal'; for these are genera, but nameless. For in general, when a genus with differentiae is predicated of something and is not its definition, the account described becomes its genus, and is predicated of several species and not of the triad alone; for genera extend more widely than their proper species, if not always in actuality, at least always in potentiality. But the things described belong to nothing other than individual triads; so the things described are the substance of the triad. For what is predicated of nothing else than the individuals under the species, and of all of them in such a way as to be predicated in the 'what it is', being assembled from the things predicated more widely in the 'what it is' of the species under which the individuals fall, this is the definition of the species predicated of the individuals. He used 'let it be supposed' instead of 'let it be laid down and agreed'; for he does not dispute about it.
p. 96b10 If, then, it belongs to nothing else.

Having sketched the method of defining for atomic species, and having shown that the definition of every atomic species is an account assembled from such things as are predicated in the 'what it is' of the individuals under the species alone, and having confirmed that the account described is the definition of the thing in question from its being predicated of the individuals under that [species] alone, he now shows that the definition of genera too is found from the species under the genus, in which the genus has its being. For since there are definitions not only of atomic species but also of genera, how shall we be able to find the definitions of genera as well, of the genera whose definitions they are? He used 'first species' and 'atomic' side by side for the same things.
p. 96b15 One should, when one is dealing with some whole.

[He says] that we find the definition of the genus through the definitions of the first and atomic species under the genus, first taking its genus (for it has a genus, if indeed it is definable), and then whatever belongs in common in the definitions of its atomic species. For the things which are common to all the species under the genus, and belong to nothing else, complete the definition of their genus; for just as what is <common> in the 'what it is' to the individuals under the species alone is the definition of the species, so too the things which belong to all the atomic species under the genus alone, being predicated in their 'what it is', complete the substance of their genus.
p. 96b25 Divisions according to the differentiae.

Having said what a definition is and how it is possible to define, he next speaks about the method of division, and shows its usefulness for finding the definition, namely for taking the things predicated universally and per se more widely, from which, when assembled and put together, the proper substance of the thing in question is made clear; for from the division according to the differentiae of the genus, a species of which we seek to define, we shall take the things predicated in the 'what it is' of the thing in question. Divisions are useful, even if they show nothing deductively, for assembling from them the 'what it is' and the definition; for this is what he called 'deducing'. They are useful also for the order of the things taken in definitions and for leaving nothing out.
p. 96b32 For if everything is from two [things], and 'tame animal' is some one thing.

That is, if in the division everything taken from the division and put together with what was divided becomes some one thing and the genus of what follows it, and the division is made from this thing that comes from the combination, it is clear that the second division will always be into fewer things, and what is narrower will not come first before what is wider in the combination of the things taken. And since the differentia taken by itself does not seem to be predicated in the 'what it is', for this reason he said that, put together with what is being divided, it becomes some one thing and is thus predicated as in the 'what it is', by this one thing becoming the genus of what follows it and being divided again. Therefore division is useful in showing this order; for what is divided will always be taken before what comes from the division.
p. 96b34 Or whatever the thing that becomes one is, one must postulate it having divided. Further, for leaving out nothing of what is in the 'what it is'.

Instead of 'one must first, having divided, postulate and take from the division what is predicated in the 'what it is' of the thing in question'; for he calls taking [something] not through demonstration 'postulating'.
p. 96b36 For when the first genus is taken.

Having shown that division is useful for the order of each of the things taken in the definition, he says that division is useful also for nothing being left out of what ought to be taken and set down in the definition. For <if> the division is made according to the differentiae proper and proximate to each genus, nothing will be left out; and the differentiae proper and proximate to the genus being divided are those into which everything under the genus being divided falls; for if the differentiae proximate to it were not taken, many things would be left out. He showed by the example which differentiae are proper and proximate and which are not proper, on account of which some things are also left out.

p. 97a2 And likewise for each of the others, both of the genera outside and of those under it, such as of bird, into which every bird [falls], and of fish, into which every fish [falls]. Proceeding in this way, then, it is possible [to know] that nothing has been left out.

'Genera outside' are either those higher and more common than animal itself, which he mentioned, or 'outside' are those different from and separate from animal and from substance, among which would be the things under the other categories. Or 'of those outside and of those under themselves' instead of 'of those not subordinate to one another but separate'; for bird and fish are such.
p. 97a5 Otherwise one must both leave [something] out and not know.
Whether it has been left out or not. Or: 'he can neither define nor have the knowledge that comes by definition'.
p. 97a6 There is no need for one who defines and divides.

Eudemus says that this opinion is Speusippus', namely that it is impossible to define any of the things that are without knowing all the things that are. And since it seems to bring some plausibility, he sets it out. For the argument that claims to show this is as follows: one who defines something must know its difference from all the things that differ from it; for what something does not differ from, it is the same as, and what it differs from, it is other than. So one who defines something as differing from the others must know its differences by which it differs from the others; for one who does not know this will think both the same to be other and the other the same. And thus he will not render the proper substance of anything either; for, as it may happen, nothing prevents the account rendered from being common to some other things too. But it is impossible to know the difference of something from some things without knowing also those things from which the thing in question differs. So one who defines something must know all things, both this thing which the definer defines (for how could he define it [otherwise]?) and all the other things from which he defines it as being other. That the argument is not sound
p. 97a11 First, then, this is false.

If something differs from something, it is not straightaway other than it; for what is other than something is not other according to every difference (for many things, though of the same species as one another, differ from one another), and it is not sound simply [to say] that things differing from one another are other, but 'in substance' must be added. For things differing in substance and by a species-making differentia are other, not those differing by any difference whatever; since in accidents too there are countless differences among things of the same species, but they are not on that account other than one another <; for if they were other than one another>, their accounts and substance would also be other.
p. 97a14 Next, when he takes the opposites and what follows.

[He shows] that one who defines something and divides, making use of the method of division, need not know all things. For when in the division he takes the opposites according to the differentiae, and takes the opposites in such a way that everything under the divided genus falls in one or other of the members opposed in the division, and it is known in which of the two the thing sought is, he will take this, even if he does not know how many and what are the things under the opposed differentiae; for it is not from knowing how many and what the <rational and the> irrational things are that it is known that man is rational, but from knowing in what being rational consists. In the same way also with the other differentiae; for if, proceeding thus according to the division made into opposites, he comes to those things of which there is no longer a differentia (and such are the atomic species), it is clear that he will have a definition from the combination of the differentiae in which he took the thing sought to be, without knowing what and how many are the things under the opposed differentiae.
p. 97a19 And that everything falls into the division, if they are opposites.
For it is not from knowing all the kinds of animals that 'every animal is either rational or irrational' becomes known, but from knowing that there is nothing between these.
p. 97a21 For everything must be in one or the other.

He did not add this idly; for a division can have been made immediate but not proper to the genus proposed; for winged-with-undivided-wing and winged-with-split-wing, even if they are immediate in the case of winged animal, will not, when combined with animal, take in all animals, because they are not proper to animal.
p. 97a23 For establishing a definition through divisions, and what follows.

Having said that the method of division is useful for giving definitions, even if not for deduction, he now says what one who wishes to establish a definition through divisions must take up and observe. By 'establish a definition' he did not mean to demonstrate [it]; for it is not possible to demonstrate a definition; for not everything that is established is also demonstrated. So by 'establish' he meant to find, put together and give [it]. He added 'through divisions'; for there are some definitions given not from division, such as those of the first genera; for it is not possible to give their accounts from division, if indeed they too are definitions. He says that those who establish and give definitions through division must aim at three things: first, to take the things predicated in the 'what it is' (these are the genus and the differentiae); second, their order, what is first and what second; third, that all these, combined, are a definition of the thing proposed, and that nothing is lacking and nothing is superfluous.
p. 97a35 That [it is] all these, is evident.
That all these, taken in such a way as to be predicated in the 'what it is', and ordered in such a way that the first follow those after them, are a definition of the thing proposed.
p. 97a37 And that of the last there is no longer a differentia.

The first thing said fits only the atomic species; for these are no longer divided by differentiae, since they are undifferentiated in species. The second thing said is more general; for it fits not only the atomic species but also the definable genera. For even if there should be, as much as you like, some dividing differentia of the things taken and combined with the first genus, still, if what we wish to define and the account given are the same in species, we divide no further.
p. 97b2 For it would be either a genus or a differentia.

That neither of these is lacking, because everything has been taken according to the continuity of the division of the genera. For there was some first genus, and this, taken together with the differentiae down to the last, produced genera; for what is divided must be divided as a genus; therefore a genus is not lacking. But neither is any differentia; for all have been taken in order, so that we have passed over none. Nor indeed has any later one that ought to be added been omitted; for the thing defined and the definition would no longer be the same in species, if some differentia were lacking, but the account given would be of some genus of the thing defined, not of this very thing which we are defining. And the genus is other than its proper species and differs in species; for things whose definitions differ are other in species; but it was laid down by us that the account given does not differ at all in species from what we are defining.
p. 97b7 One must inquire by looking at.

Having spoken in between about the method of division and shown its usefulness for definitions, he returns to what was said earlier; this was that one must take the definition of the genus from the definition of the atomic species under the genus; for he said: "for to those who combine [them] from the atomic [species], what follows from the definitions will be clear". He joins this to those [words] and shows how, by using the manner stated before, we shall be able to recognize the definitions of common things and things that have the appearance of genera but are not genera. For there are some things which, because they have received some common name, seem to be of the same genus while being homonymous, as 'being' is a common name, but no longer a common thing; and similarly 'the good'. The one defining must not take any of these as a genus. So how we shall be able to guard against this he teaches through these [words], and how we shall find the definition of genera from the species. This he has already said above too; for the finding of definitions begins from below, as he describes.
p. 97b24 But if none, there would be two species of pride.
He said this not taking [them] as species of a genus (for thus pride too would be a genus having two species), but because 'pride' is homonymous.
p. 97b26 Every definition is always universal.
Having determined what accompanies definitions, he also says what those who define must aim at.
p. 97b28 Therefore one must pass from the particulars to the universals.

By 'particulars' he means not the individual and the truly atomic (he would be saying things in conflict with what was said before), but the atomic species; for this is the particular among definable things; for it is particular as definable, not simply. He himself showed this too by saying 'or in undifferentiated things'; for things no longer divided into species are undifferentiated with respect to differentiae in the strict sense. It is easier to define the atomic species, because the things of which it is predicated are more evident than the species of which the genus is predicated. And it was shown that the definition of what is predicated is gathered from the commonness and sameness of the subjects. So if the definitions of species are better known than those of genera, one must pass from the species to the definition of the genera in the way stated, not dividing from above but combining from below.
p. 97b29 For homonymies also escape notice more.

For because the things underlying the atomic species are more evident, homonymy in them is easy to recognize. So if those defining must guard against homonymies, and these are more easily guarded against in the species, for this reason too one must make the start of definitions from the species.
p. 97b31 Just as in demonstrations.

That just as in demonstrations deducing certainly comes first (for a demonstration cannot be non-deductive), so also in [definitions] there must be clarity; for an unclear account is not a definition, if indeed a definition professes to make the thing sought known.
p. 97b35 And so to proceed to the common.

That one must not try to give a definition of something homonymous. Besides this he says that it also contributes to clarity to give definitions through proper names and not use metaphors or figurative words; for such things, being able to fit many things, are causes of unclarity. By 'converse' he means to discourse dialectically.
p. 98a1 With a view to having the problems.

Through these [words] he hands down to us a method by which we shall be able to be well supplied for stating problems. To state problems is both to be able to put them forward and to give their causes, and it is in this sense that he himself now uses 'state', namely for stating the causes of the things sought, as he will also show as he proceeds; for he calls problems those in which the 'why' is sought [by] the method he hands down. † Or both are shown at once, both the finding of problems and the finding of the cause. He has many books of such problems. So how we shall be well supplied for giving the cause in things put forward, he describes; for what he now says is not about definitions, as some thought.
p. 98a13 Now, then, [we have spoken] according to the common names handed down.

He says that the selection stated before is useful for giving the cause in problems not only in the case of things having a common and single name predicated [of them], but also in those where the common [feature] is not one and the same, but has its sameness by analogy. For when things that are different and are in different [subjects] have the same analogy, all the things in which they are also become in a way common, not simply but by analogy. For there is not one common [feature] in things having cuttlebone, bone and fish-spine, as in things having horns there was the one [feature] 'horned', but the one is taken in their case by analogy; for the ratio that bone has in footed animals, fish-spine has in fishes and cuttlebone in cuttlefish; for each of them is a kind of support in each of the things in which it is.
p. 98a24 Some problems are the same by having the same middle.

What sort of problems are the same: either those of which the cause and middle is the same, and this is either the same in genus alone or the same both in genus and in species; or those of which the cause is under the other cause, that is, the cause of the one is under the cause of the other. Next he also sets down the [sameness] by analogy. Through these he teaches us how we shall recognise all the problems that, though they are the same as one another, do not seem so because they are asked about different matter, so that, having become well supplied with the cause for one of them, we are able to speak likewise about the others too. Theophrastus also worked on the collection of similar problems. But he in those [works] records which of the problems are similar to one another; whereas Aristotle now teaches by what we shall judge problems that are the same as one another. He says, then, that they are the same as one another in two ways: either by having the same middle, for example that all are counter-displacement. In such problems the common middle is the counter-displacement of the hot, for example: why do we digest better in winter? Why do we breathe densely when asleep? Why are springs warmer in winter? For of all these the cause is the same, the counter-displacement of the hot, which is also the middle term. And again, of these problems that are the same through having the same middle, he makes a certain subdivision before stating the second way, according to which problems also become the same as one another; for of those having the same cause and middle, some are the same in genus but not in species, while others are the same in species in addition to genus.
p. 98a35 One might raise a difficulty about the cause and that of which it is the cause.

He has already spoken about causes coexisting with what is caused; for he showed that the causes of things that are, are; of things that have come to be, have come to be; of things that will be, will be; and of things coming to be, are coming to be. Now he raises a difficulty of this sort about this very point: it is laid down and has been shown that the cause is the middle term in a demonstration; moreover this too is agreed, that if the middle is, it is wholly necessary that the conclusion also is, so that if the cause is, what is caused, which is the conclusion, must also be. With this laid down, he asks whether it converts, so that if what is caused, which was the conclusion, is, the cause too, which was the middle, is of necessity. The solution is that, if the cause posited and taken for it does not coexist with what is caused when it is, something else and not that would be its cause; for when what is caused is, there must be the cause through which it is; but if it does coexist, the proof will be circular, and the same thing will be at one time cause and at another what is caused.
p. 98b16 But if it is not possible for things to be causes of one another.

That if it is not possible for things to be causes of one another (for the cause is prior to that of which it is the cause, if not in time, then in [nature]), and it is agreed that the cause of the moon's being eclipsed is the earth's being in the middle, whereas the eclipse is not the cause of the earth's being in the middle, and if the demonstration through the cause is of the 'why', while that not through the cause is of the 'that', it is clear that the other proof, the one that concludes the cause, does not come about through the cause; for that the earth is in the middle one knows through the eclipse, but why, not. So they are not demonstrated through one another; for demonstration is through a cause.

Having said this and resolved the difficulty that seemed to follow once it was laid down that the cause coexists with what is caused, he showed that he had taken it readily to assume that what is caused follows the cause, [and] that if the cause did not also follow and coexist with what is caused, there would be another cause of it and not the one laid down, <because> what is caused and the conclusion is upon some middle and is in every case. So what could have been brought against that proof, he puts forward and tries to state: or is it possible for there to be several causes of one thing? For if this is possible, it is not of necessity that the cause, upon whose positing [what is caused] followed, converts with what is caused. For what is caused converts in every case with some cause, but not in every case with this one through which it was shown, if it is possible for there to be several causes of the same thing. For with each of the causes taken as middle the conclusion and what is caused will follow of necessity, but not, if the conclusion and what is caused is, will this cause too already be of necessity, because there can also be another cause of it, if indeed there are several causes of the same thing. [Having raised the difficulty whether it is perhaps possible for there to be several causes of the same thing, he next sets down how it is possible for the same thing to belong to several things according to different causes, thereby showing and establishing that it is possible to say there are several causes of the same thing.]
p. 98b19 If then the demonstration through the cause is of the 'why'.

If that through which the being and the substance is known is a cause, while what is not so is not a cause, and of these the one is known through the other, but no longer the reverse, they would not be convertible as causes of one another.
p. 98b23 Or is it possible for there to be several causes of one thing?

Having raised the difficulty whether it is perhaps possible for there to be several causes of the same thing, namely according to the same mode of cause, he sets down how the same thing can belong to several things according to several causes, thereby showing and establishing that it is possible to say there are several causes of the same thing; for if there are several causes of the same thing's belonging to several things, it is also possible for there to be several causes of the same thing. And he shows that it is not possible for the same thing to belong to the same thing through several causes. For refuting this he takes [the point] that the problem is always universal; for in problems one seeks the cause not of something's belonging to this individual, but of its belonging universally to these things and being able to belong. For he who seeks the cause of animal, insofar as it is animal, belonging to certain things seeks some common cause, according to which it belongs to all to which it belongs; for the cause and that of which it is the cause, that is, what is caused, must both belong universally to something, to which it belongs and to which it is able to belong. And for this reason it belongs first and per se to the common [item] and to the genus, if there is some genus alike of each of them, and then through the same cause to all its species too, <if there are> species in which what is caused and the cause and middle convert. Having shown that in all the cases where what is caused [is], the cause too [is], he did away with its being possible for there to be several causes of the same thing in the stated way. For if there were one cause of A's belonging to D, for example B, as he took it, and another again of A's belonging to E, for example C, the cause will not be predicated universally of those things of which A, which is what is caused, is predicated. And in this way what has been given will not even be the cause of what is sought in the problem.
p. 99a1 But is it possible for the cause not to be the same?

Having shown that it is not possible for the same thing to belong to the same thing through several causes (for that to which the universal belongs first, it belongs to through one cause; and that through which [it belongs] to this, through this it also [belongs] to each of the things under this), he now asks, about the example he put forward for the same thing's being able to belong to several things through different causes, how it stands and whether this is possible. For example, if animal is shown to belong to man through one middle and to eagle through another; for there will seem to be several causes of animal's belonging to the things it belongs to: for some the winged, for others the footed, for others the aquatic. Resolving this, then, and pointing out that 'cause' is twofold (for the cause of the conclusion is not in every case also the cause of the thing), showing this he says that if it has been demonstrated per se, that is, if the proof comes about through the cause which is the cause of the thing, the same cause must be taken in all cases in which the same thing is shown to belong. He set out the reason for this, which he has already shown, saying 'for the cause through which it is shown is a definition of the extreme that is predicated and belongs to the several things, and this is the middle term'; for such a cause belongs to the several things according to something common and the same. But if it is demonstrated not through the cause but through a sign, or through an accident taken as middle, it is possible for the same thing to be shown to belong to one thing through one [middle] and to another through another.
p. 99a2 Or, if it has been demonstrated per se and not by way of a sign.
The sign always accompanies the thing; but the accident can also <be> external [to it].
p. 99a6 Otherwise the middle will be alike: if [they are] homonymous.

But if it is not demonstrated per se, nor through things that belong per se, the middle will be alike, in the way that the thing whose cause is sought is too. He added this because he had shown that the cause, the thing of which it is the cause, and that to which [it belongs] can be taken not per se but by accident or as a sign. Having said that such things do not seem to be problems, he added 'otherwise', in place of 'but if these too were investigated as problems', the middle will be alike: if what is caused is homonymous, the cause too will be of that kind; if [it is] as in a genus, the cause too [will be] of that kind; likewise also if [it is] by analogy.
p. 99a16 The cause's following on one another is like this.

He said 'the following on is like this' in place of 'it is like this concerning the following on'. And he has used 'follow on' in place of 'convert'. The construction of the phrase is this: the cause, that of which it is the cause, and that to which it is the cause follow on one another in this way. That to which it is the cause is the subject, and that of which it is the cause is what belongs to this. He says this about the causes in demonstrations. Having said in what preceded that the cause of the thing, and not the cause of the conclusion, and that of which it is the cause follow on one another, because the cause is a definition of what is caused (for he had already said this earlier, and will say it now too; he has used this to show that the same thing cannot be shown demonstratively to belong to several things through different causes), and having used also the fact that both the cause and what is caused are predicated universally of something, he now says when that of which both what is caused and the cause are predicated per se converts with them, with the cause and with what is caused; for [he says] the terms convert, in the cases where circular proof also comes about.
p. 99a18 For one taking each individually, that of which [it is] the cause.

That the cause, that of which it is the cause, and that to which it is the cause, which is the subject term, follow on one another and convert, [holds] not always; but if we take the subject term, of which we seek the cause of something's belonging to it, species by species, that whose belonging we seek the cause of will be wider; [but taking] the things to which the predicate belongs [all together], both the subject term and the predicate term will be equal [in extension], and the middle and cause will be alike. For as the predicate is related to the subject, so too is the cause; for the cause has been shown to be a definition of the predicate. By 'first middle' he means the cause proximate to the predicate, of which there is no further middle, which he also called the first extreme itself.
p. 99a21 The first middle is an account of the first extreme.

For this reason all the sciences too come about through definition; for all demonstrate the things that fall under them; and demonstrations are through the cause; and the cause is an account and definition of the first extreme; for they use the definitions of the first things for the demonstrations of what comes after them.
p. 99a23 For example, shedding leaves follows the vine at the same time.

He teaches how the first middle is a definition of the first extreme, and why he added 'first' to 'middle'. For shedding leaves is shown to belong to all leaf-shedding things through two middles, both through being broad-leaved and through the moisture's congealing. The middle proximate to the subject is being broad-leaved, which he called the first middle in one direction; and [the one proximate] to the predicate, to shedding leaves, is the congealing of the moisture, which is also a definition of the predicate and first middle as being nearer the predication and being its cause and definition. But for one starting from below, from the subject, the first middle is what is common to all such things; this is being broad-leaved; for this shows what sort of things the leaf-shedding things are. And again, the middle between this common [item] and shedding leaves is the moisture's congealing, which is the cause and definition of shedding leaves.
p. 99a30 In the case of the figures he will render it thus.

He has spoken about the sequence of terms in demonstrations and about universal terms, in which the cause prior to the thing is taken, which was also a definition of what is predicated in the problem. And having shown which of the subjects convert with both the cause and what is caused, and which do not, he shows this same thing with terms and deductions, making what has been shown more knowable and more credible by setting out the terms.
p. 99a35 But all together they convert and extend beyond.

That is: for this is what I now call universal. For of what is predicated universally, one kind is equal [in extension], which also converts; and he called it 'first universal', with which the individual [species] do not convert, but all together do convert; and this is what is predicated not through some middle but primarily; the other kind is not equal, per se indeed, but not primarily, rather through a middle.
p. 99a36 So A must extend more widely than B.

That is: but if A is predicated more widely than B, this [B] would no longer be its cause; for why this rather than something else, through which [A] is predicated both of D itself and of certain others besides those of which B is predicated? And how this is so he shows next.
p. 99a37 If, then, A belongs to all the E's.

What he says is this: if A belongs not only to all the D's, to which it was shown to belong through B, but also to the E's, all the E's will be other than B, that is, not under B; for B is predicated only of the D's. For if the E's do not fall outside B, A would no longer be taken more widely than both the E's and the D's, if the E's were the same as the D's, all being under B. He showed this by saying 'for otherwise, how will it be possible to say that A [belongs] to everything to which E [belongs], but E not to everything to which A [belongs]?' For in this way A becomes wider than E, if A [belongs] to every E but does not also convert; and this will be so if it <is> belonging to more things than B. For if [it belongs] only to those of which E is predicated, it will be equal to the things of which it is predicated, they being under B, so that E too [belongs] to every A. Likewise also in the case of D. Having said this and shown that E will not be under B, he adds: 'for why will there not be some cause, as [B was] of A to D?' This is equivalent to 'for why is there not some cause of A's belonging also to the E's, just as there was a cause of its belonging to the D's, namely B?' He says this explaining what he said and giving the reason for 'otherwise, why will this be the cause rather than that?' For if A also belongs to the E's, which are other than the D's, it will belong to these too through some cause. For he said 'as A to D' in place of 'of the kind as when A was shown to belong to the D's'; for it was shown to belong through B as middle. To which he added 'so the E's too will at the same time be some one thing'. So likewise the E's too will be some one thing, that is, there will be one thing under which [they fall] and which is predicated of all of them, as the D's were under B. If, then, the E's are under some one thing, let us in turn examine this. And if we find whatever that is <which> again is the cause of A's belonging to the E's, let this be C, which belongs to all the E's, and A to all of it.
p. 99b4 It is possible, then, for there to be several causes of the same thing.

Having shown that, when the predicate is said more widely, it is not impossible in a deduction for the same thing to be concluded, through several causes and middles, as belonging to things that differ in species, he adds that it is possible for there to be several causes of the same thing, but not for things that are the same in species; for substance belongs to animal through one cause and to stone through another. This is possible in the case of the causes of the conclusion in a deduction, about which he is now speaking; for he said 'if the deduction comes about through accidents and signs'. But in the case of demonstrations and deductions through the cause it was shown to be impossible; for such a cause was the definition of the predicate, which is the same also for things differing in species as the cause of the genus belonging to them; for animal belongs both to horse and to man, demonstratively, through the perceptive.
p. 99b5 Quadrupeds by not having bile.

So long-lived will be said in several ways. For things of whose belonging there are several causes are said in several ways, if indeed the cause is the definition of what is caused; for of that which has several causes there are also several accounts, not as indicating the same thing; and that which has several accounts in this way is among the things said in several ways.
p. 99b7 But if they do not come at once to the atomic.

For the middles are causes as in a deduction. In this way there will also be several deductions, and the middles will have the same order towards one another as the middle had towards the predicate when the conclusion was shown through one middle; for the higher of the middles and causes have the order of things predicated and can be said more widely, for example substance, ensouled, perceptive, footed, rational, man.
p. 99b9 Which of the middles is the cause: the one first towards the universal?

That, of conclusions that have several middles, the nearest to each is the cause of the universal's belonging to it. For having said that where the middles are several the causes too are several, as many as the middles, he next inquires, of conclusions that have several middles, which is more their cause: the one first towards the universal, that is, towards the first predicated term, of which the first predicate, when taken, makes the first universal premise; or the one towards the last and subject, which he called atomic, being either truly atomic or an atomic species. 'For the particulars' he would say in place of 'of the first universal's belonging to the particulars'. He says that the nearest to each is the cause of the universal's belonging to it, and adds the reason: 'for of the first' (calling first what he called atomic and last subject) of this being under the first and universal term the middle proximate to it is the cause. For C is the cause for D of B's belonging to it, on account of which A too belongs to it. Hence C is the cause of A's belonging to D, for this is proximate to it; and again B of A's belonging to C, for again B is proximate to C. But A belongs to B no longer through another middle, if it should be a middle. For he said this by 'and to this [it belongs] in itself'; for if it is its definition, it would no longer belong to it through another middle.
p. 99b15 About deduction and demonstration, then.

He added 'demonstrative' to 'knowledge', since knowledge is more common and is predicated of other things too. He did not further mention separately the treatment of definition, about which too he has spoken in this [book], since it also contributes to the generation and constitution of demonstrations. For he speaks of definitions principally in Book Z of the Metaphysics; for the most authoritative demonstration, the one through the reason why, has been shown to come about through the definition of the predicated extreme.
p. 99b17 About the principles, how they become known.

He inquires about the demonstrative principles (these are the immediate and first premises), how they become known, since not through demonstration and deduction, and what state or capacity of the soul it is that knows them.
p. 99b32 It is necessary, then, to have some capacity.

Resolving the difficulty, he does <not> concede, as absurd, that we have knowledge of the principles from birth, and tries to say how we acquire it later. And since it is impossible for any learning to come about without some pre-existing knowledge, and it is also absurd that there should always be some principles of the principles more known than those after them, he says how, with some knowledge present in us, the knowledge of the principles arises later and this does not proceed to infinity. For it is necessary that we have some capacity pre-existing the knowledge of the principles, from which the knowledge of these comes about (for otherwise it is impossible), but that this is not such as will be more honourable than these by being more precise, as the knowledge of the principles of knowledge is more honourable than [the knowledge of the things] after it, the knowledge of which comes about through them. For a principle of that kind, through which something is shown, is more authoritative for knowledge and more precise than what becomes known through it; but a principle that is such as a kind of underlying capacity, having the role of matter towards what is constituted from it and upon it, is not more precise than what comes about and is constituted upon it, nor in this respect more honourable; for the incomplete is not more precise than the complete, since neither is matter [more precise] than form.
p. 99b39 In those in which it is possible, when they perceive, still to have [something] in the soul.

That <there are> those in which there is a capacity to preserve the percept and to have something in the soul after perceiving, after the perception; and there are those that are able also to preserve as some one thing in the soul what comes from the many, and that are likewise active in perception and rational. For in those in which there is greater cognition of the affection from perception, some acquire an account from the memory and persistence of several perceptibles, others do not. For according to the difference of the soul receiving the percept a proper structure arises from the memories derived from perceptibles. For from the percept and the persistence of what was actually perceived [come] memory and imagination. For imagination is a certain motion of the soul produced by what remains from perception; for the imaginative soul, attending to this residue, which is also called the object of imagination, as to a perceptible that is within, is somehow altered, as perception is by the perceptible that is outside. When it attends to it as to something previously seen and as to something like it, it remembers; and the state and the apprehension of it that comes about as of an image and likeness of it is memory. But if [it attends] not as to such a thing, and does not bring along with it that it is an image and likeness of what it previously perceived, such a thing is imagination, but no longer memory.
p. 100a6 And from experience, the universal having come to rest.

'The universal having come to rest' in place of 'it having remained the same and in the same way and been thought, and not having its transition as to many things but having remained as one thing in the soul'. What the universal is we shall explain: the one over all the particulars and many things, taken in the soul according to the likeness and sameness in them, this is the universal. This universal becomes the principle of art and knowledge. For experience is still unfixed; but the universal premise is fixed and stays the same, and from the likeness of the things that have come under perception and memory, and from the experience of these, it makes a like comprehension also of things similar to these that have not come into perception, as † [...] all of these too having [it] by the transition from like to like.
'Being about coming-to-be', that is, being about what is generated and made. What is made, not simply but made by us, is the principle of art.

'But if about what is'. Either he means knowledge about what is ungenerated and eternal and not in coming-to-be; for it was shown that knowledge and demonstrations are about eternal things. Or rather he would call 'what is' that of which the apprehension came about as of something that is, not as of something coming about through us; for the persistence of the universal from such a thing, out of memory and experience, is the principle of knowledge. For natural science too [is knowledge], although it is about moving things and about coming-to-be; for simply, art is about what comes about through us, which is why the principle of its being is in us, while knowledge is about things that do not come about through us but are.
p. 100a13 'And the soul is such as to be able to undergo this.'

So too in the soul, which has the rational power, there occurs such a halt within it. For out of perceptibles flowing past and coming to be different at different times, memory arises, and experience from memory, and upon this a halt of the universal that rests upon this experience, then of another similar one, and so the advance from such halts and comprehensions [proceeds] to the universal and the principle. As for 'until it came to a principle', he said it either of the things thought and gathered together in the soul; for the joint perception and formation <of the> universal upon perceptibles, and the grasp of universals upon the first ones, is a grasp of the principle and of the first common thing. Or by 'principle' he meant, in the army too, the rallying and the order and the gathering and the drawing up in line of the whole army. And he says that the soul has a fitness and power for being able to preserve the affections from perceptibles.
p. 100a14 'What was said long ago.'
When he said 'from experience, the universal having come to rest in the soul'.
p. 100a16 'For one perceives the particular.'

He says that perception perceives what it perceives in the case of particulars; for perception is perceptive of things in particulars and atomic things; but the apprehension itself comes to be of the universal. Wishing to show how this comes about, he used as example man and Callias, not as though man qua man or Callias qua Callias were perceptible, but through these he makes known what he means. For as one who has a notion of man has the notion not as of Callias the man or of some one of the particulars, but of that which is predicated in common of all particular men, being in all of them, so sight, perceiving the white in snow, does not perceive it as white snow but as white; and this white is common to the snow and to all white things; for it sees the white in it, but not qua snow.
p. 100b2 'For example, such-and-such an animal.'
What is said with some addition is divided, for example 'such-and-such an animal'; what is said without addition is partless, that is, not divided.
p. 100b5 'Since of the states concerned with thought.'

[He shows] that the knowledge of principles is not the same as knowledge through demonstration, and that intellect is what knows the principles of knowledge; and that, the intellect in us being twofold, one theoretical and the other practical, and the practical being about things contingent and able to be otherwise, while the theoretical is about eternal things that are always alike, the powers of the practical intellect are the opinative and the calculative, and of the theoretical the intellective and the scientific; of which those of the practical are not always true, but those of the theoretical always. And [he shows] that opinion is supposition without demonstration, which is why it is also unstable, and calculation is often deceived because the matter it is about does not admit of exact knowledge; for it is about contingent things, which are also the objects of wishing. For the senses are true in another way, not by some combination; for this is proper to the rational soul.
p. 100b15 'And the principle would be of the principle.'

Having said that intellect is the principle of knowledge, and that the objects of knowledge also have principles, the immediate premises, he now says that the principle of knowledge would be the cognition of the principle of the objects of knowledge, while knowledge as a whole [is cognition] of the whole object of knowledge; for as the principle is to the principle, so the whole, of which it is the principle, is to the whole matter whose principle the principle of knowledge was cognitive and contemplative of.
